text:
CYRANO:
  That is possible.
  But one does not abdicate the honor of being a target.
  (Cards, dice, smoke subside, fall, fly away with increasing
  satisfaction):
  Had I been present when the sash slipped off
  —Our courage, sir, differs in this respect—
  I would have picked it up and put it on.

DE GUICHE:
  Yes, more Gascon boasting!

CYRANO:
  Boasting?...
  Lend it to me. I offer to go up, this very evening,
  First into the assault, with it across my chest.

DE GUICHE:
  Another Gascon offer! You know that the sash
  Remained with the enemy, on the banks of the Scarpe,
  In a place that grapeshot has since riddled—
  Where no one can go to retrieve it!

CYRANO (drawing the white sash from his pocket and holding it out to him):
  Here it is.
  (Silence. The cadets stifle their laughter in their cards and in their
  dice cups. De Guiche turns around and looks at them: they immediately
  resume their gravity, their games; one of them whistles with
  indifference the mountain tune played by the fife.)

DE GUICHE (taking the sash):
  Thank you. With this scrap of light-colored cloth, I shall
  Be able to give a signal—which I was hesitating to give.
  (He goes to the embankment, climbs it, and waves the sash several times in the air.)

ALL:
  Eh!

THE SENTRY (at the top of the embankment):
  That man down there, running away!...

DE GUICHE (coming back down):
  He is a sham Spanish spy. He renders us
  Great services. The information he carries
  To the enemy is what I give him, so
  That their decisions can be influenced.

CYRANO:
  He is a scoundrel!

DE GUICHE (nonchalantly tying on his sash):
  It is very convenient. What were we saying?...
  —Ah! I was about to tell you something. This very night,
  Attempting one supreme stroke to resupply us,
  The marshal went off toward Dourlens, without drums;
  The King's sutlers are there; across the plowed fields
  He will join them; but in order to return without mishap,
  He took so many troops with him
  That anyone attacking us would certainly have an easy time of it:
  Half the army is absent from the camp!

CARBON:
  Yes, if the Spaniards knew, it would be serious.
  But they do not know of this departure?

DE GUICHE:
  They know.
  They are going to attack us.

CARBON:
  Ah!

DE GUICHE:
  My sham spy
  Came to warn me of their assault.
  He added: “I can determine its location;
  At what point do you want the attack to take place?
  I shall say that it is the least defended of all,
  And the force of the attack will fall upon it.”—I answered:
  “Very well. Leave the camp. Keep your eyes on the line:
  It will be at the point from which I signal to you.”

CARBON (to the cadets):
  Gentlemen, prepare yourselves!
  (They all rise. Sound of swords and sword belts being buckled.)

DE GUICHE:
  It will be in an hour.

FIRST CADET:
  Ah!... very well!...
  (They all sit down again. The interrupted game resumes.)

DE GUICHE (to Carbon):
  We must gain time. The marshal is returning.

CARBON:
  And to gain time?

DE GUICHE:
  You will be so kind
  As to have yourselves killed.

CYRANO:
  Ah! So that is the revenge?

DE GUICHE:
  I shall not claim that, if I loved you,
  I would have chosen you and your men; but,
  Since no courage compares with yours,
  It is my King I serve by serving my rancor.

CYRANO (saluting):
  Allow me to be grateful to you, sir.

DE GUICHE (saluting):
  I know that you like to fight one against a hundred.
  You will not complain of lacking work.
  (He climbs back up, with Carbon.)

CYRANO (to the cadets):
  Well then! To Gascony's coat of arms,
  Which bears six chevrons, gentlemen, azure and gold,
  We are going to add a chevron of blood that it still lacked!
  (De Guiche speaks in a low voice with Carbon de Castel-Jaloux, at the rear. Orders
  are given. The defense is prepared. Cyrano goes toward Christian, who has
  remained motionless, his arms folded.)

CYRANO (putting his hand on Christian's shoulder):
  Christian?

CHRISTIAN (shaking his head):
  Roxane!

CYRANO:
  Alas!

CHRISTIAN:
  At least, I would like to put
  All my heart's farewell into a beautiful letter!...

CYRANO:
  I suspected that it would be today.
  (He draws a note from his doublet):
  And I have written your farewells.

CHRISTIAN:
  Show me!...

CYRANO:
  You want to?...

CHRISTIAN (taking the letter from him):
  Why, yes!
  (He opens it, reads, and stops):
  Look!

CYRANO:
  What?

CHRISTIAN:
  This little circle?...

CYRANO (quickly taking back the letter and looking at it with an innocent air):
  A circle?...

CHRISTIAN:
  It is a tear!

CYRANO:
  Yes... A poet gets caught up in his own game—that is the charm!...
  You understand... this note—it was very moving:
  I made myself weep while writing it.

CHRISTIAN:
  Weep?...

CYRANO:
  Yes... because... dying is not terrible.
  But... never seeing her again... that is what is horrible!
  For after all I do not...
  (Christian looks at him):
  we do not...
  (Quickly):
  you do not...

CHRISTIAN (snatching the letter from him):
  Give me that note!
  (A commotion is heard in the distance, in the camp.)

A SENTRY'S VOICE:
  By God's belly, who goes there?
  (Gunshots. Sounds of voices. Jingle bells.)

CARBON:
  What is it?...

THE SENTRY (who is on the embankment):
  A carriage!
  (They rush to look.)

SHOUTS:
  What! In the camp?—It is coming in!
  —It looks as though it comes from the enemy!—The devil!
  Fire!—No! The coachman shouted!—Shouted what?—
  He shouted: On the King's service!
  (Everyone is on the embankment, looking outside. The jingle bells draw
  nearer.)

DE GUICHE:
  Eh? The King!...
  (They come back down and form ranks.)

CARBON:
  Hats off, everyone!

DE GUICHE (offstage):
  The King!—Stand aside, vile rabble,
  So that it may describe its curve with pomp!
  (The carriage enters at a fast trot. It is covered with mud and
  dust. The curtains are drawn. Two lackeys stand behind. It stops dead.)

CARBON (shouting):
  Beat the salute!
  (Roll of drums. All the cadets uncover their heads.)

DE GUICHE:
  Lower the step!
  (Two men rush forward. The carriage door opens.)

ROXANE (jumping from the carriage):
  Good day!
  (The sound of a woman's voice makes all these deeply bowed men
  straighten up at once.—Astonishment.)
